reason: This passage from Nehemiah 5 portrays regular people (the common laborers and families) as sympathetically victimized by unjust economic systems yet fundamentally virtuous. Their complaints about debt slavery and oppression are presented as legitimate grievances rather than unfounded. Critically, when confronted with the problem by Nehemiah, they respond to righteous leadership by immediately ceasing their exploitation of one another, saying 'Amen' and praising God while committing to reform. They are depicted as responsive to moral correction and obedient to just authority, contrasting sharply with the earlier governors and nobles who exploited them. The portrayal emphasizes their suffering and lack of agency, but not their moral failing—rather, they are shown as fundamentally good people trapped in systemic oppression who readily embrace justice when offered.
